questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: Define standard enthalpy of formation and standard enthalpy of combustion. Write a balanced equation, including state symbols, for the standard formation of liquid water. [5 marks]
markPoints: Standard formation enthalpy is the enthalpy change when exactly one mole of a compound is formed.
The compound forms from its constituent elements in their standard states under standard conditions.
Standard combustion enthalpy is the enthalpy change when exactly one mole of a substance is completely burned in oxygen.
For standard combustion, substances are in their standard states under standard conditions.
The correctly balanced one-mole formation equation is H₂(g)+½O₂(g)→H₂O(l).
questions.modelAnswer: Standard formation enthalpy is the enthalpy change when exactly one mole of a compound is formed. The compound forms from its constituent elements in their standard states under standard conditions. Standard combustion enthalpy is the enthalpy change when exactly one mole of a substance is completely burned in oxygen. For standard combustion, substances are in their standard states under standard conditions. The correctly balanced one-mole formation equation is H₂(g)+½O₂(g)→H₂O(l).

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: 25.0 cm³ of 2.00 mol dm⁻³ HCl reacts with 25.0 cm³ of 2.00 mol dm⁻³ NaOH. Temperature rises by 13.4°C. Assume density 1.00 g cm⁻³ and specific heat capacity 4.18 J g⁻¹ K⁻¹. Calculate the molar enthalpy change of neutralisation, with its correct sign. [6 marks]
markPoints: The total solution volume is 25.0+25.0=50.0 cm³.
Mass of solution is 50.0 g from density 1.00 g cm⁻³.
Amount reacted is 0.0500 mol from 2.00×0.0250 for both HCl and NaOH in a 1:1 neutralisation.
Convert q_solution to 2.8006 kJ and divide by 0.0500 mol to obtain a magnitude 56.0 kJ mol⁻¹.
Final reaction enthalpy is ΔH=−56.0 kJ mol⁻¹ because the solution warmed and the reaction released heat.
questions.modelAnswer: The total solution volume is 25.0+25.0=50.0 cm³. Mass of solution is 50.0 g from density 1.00 g cm⁻³. Using q=mcΔT gives q_solution=50.0×4.18×13.4=2800.6 J. Amount reacted is 0.0500 mol from 2.00×0.0250 for both HCl and NaOH in a 1:1 neutralisation. Convert q_solution to 2.8006 kJ and divide by 0.0500 mol to obtain a magnitude 56.0 kJ mol⁻¹. Final reaction enthalpy is ΔH=−56.0 kJ mol⁻¹ because the solution warmed and the reaction released heat.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.prompt: Estimate ΔH for H₂(g)+Cl₂(g)→2HCl(g) using these tabulated bond enthalpies in kJ mol⁻¹: H–H=436, Cl–Cl=243 and H–Cl=431. Show all bonds broken and formed, give the signed result, and explain why the result is approximate. [6 marks]
markPoints: One H–H bond must be broken.
One Cl–Cl bond must be broken.
Total energy needed to break bonds is 436+243=679 kJ mol⁻¹ for the reaction as written.
Two H–Cl bonds form and release an energy magnitude of 2×431=862 kJ mol⁻¹.
Reaction enthalpy estimate is 679−862=−183 kJ mol⁻¹.
Tabulated bond enthalpies may be rounded approximations; H₂, Cl₂ and HCl are diatomic, so averaging across differing molecular environments is not needed for these particular bonds.
questions.modelAnswer: One H–H bond must be broken. One Cl–Cl bond must be broken. Total energy needed to break bonds is 436+243=679 kJ mol⁻¹ for the reaction as written. Two H–Cl bonds form and release an energy magnitude of 2×431=862 kJ mol⁻¹. Reaction enthalpy estimate is 679−862=−183 kJ mol⁻¹. Tabulated bond enthalpies may be rounded approximations; H₂, Cl₂ and HCl are diatomic, so averaging across differing molecular environments is not needed for these particular bonds.
